name: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
title: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
answer: Citation auditing and good law checking is the process of verifying that every authority cited in a legal document remains valid, has not been overruled or reversed, and still supports the proposition for which it is cited. It applies to case law, statutes, regulations, and secondary sources. In AI-related litigation, this work must account for a fast-moving body of authority, including the 142 active AI lawsuits and 29 AI case law precedents tracked on this site. The goal is to ensure that a brief or motion does not rely on a decision that has been silently undermined.

sections.body: Citation auditing and good law checking is the process of verifying that every authority cited in a legal document remains valid, has not been overruled or reversed, and still supports the proposition for which it is cited. It applies to case law, statutes, regulations, and secondary sources. In AI-related litigation, this work must account for a fast-moving body of authority, including the 142 active AI lawsuits and 29 AI case law precedents tracked on this site. The goal is to ensure that a brief or motion does not rely on a decision that has been silently undermined.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Citation auditing runs on legal research platforms that maintain structured databases of court opinions, statutes, and citator histories. These systems ingest new decisions, extract citation relationships, and update treatment flags such as overruled, reversed, or distinguished. The infrastructure relies on document parsing, entity recognition for case names and citations, and graph databases that connect citing and cited authorities. For AI-specific questions, the site's 210 compliance and regulation pages and 6838 state AI bills provide a parallel source for checking whether a cited statute or rule has changed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A researcher takes each citation in a draft and runs it through a citator to see its subsequent history and treatment. They look for direct negative signals such as overruled, reversed, or abrogated, and for indirect signals such as criticized, distinguished, or narrowed. The checker then reads the later authority to confirm whether the original proposition still holds for the specific point being made. In AI matters, this may mean checking whether a cited decision has been affected by one of the 142 active AI lawsuits or by a newer decision among the 29 tracked precedents.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Citation checking is a professional responsibility matter, because courts can sanction attorneys for citing bad law and a missed negative treatment can damage a client's position. Provenance requires that each citation trace to an official or authenticated source, not a summary, headnote, or third-party paraphrase. The site's 674 glossary terms and 732 AI tools can help a researcher understand what an AI-related citation means, but the authoritative source remains the court or legislature. Risk includes relying on an automated flag without reading the underlying decision, or citing a case that has been vacated, depublished, or superseded by statute.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Citation auditing is moving from one-time checks before filing toward continuous monitoring that alerts a team when a cited authority changes status. AI systems are beginning to extract the holding of a case and compare it against later treatment, flagging not only formal reversal but also substantive erosion of a proposition. For AI law, the rapid growth of state AI bills and new precedents means citation status can change quickly, and tools will likely integrate legislative and regulatory updates alongside case citators. The site's tracking of 6838 state AI bills and 210 compliance pages points toward a future where good law checking includes pending legislation that may affect the authority of a cited statute.
